question_text:
A 12-year-old girl is presented to the office by her mother with complaints of cola-colored urine and mild facial puffiness that began 5 days ago. According to her mother, she had a sore throat 3 weeks ago. Her immunization records are up to date. The mother denies fever and any change in bowel habits. The vital signs include blood pressure 138/78 mm Hg, pulse 88/min, temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), and respiratory rate 11/min. On physical examination, there is pitting edema of the upper and lower extremities bilaterally. An oropharyngeal examination is normal. Urinalysis shows the following results:
pH 6.2
Color dark brown
Red blood cell (RBC) count 18–20/HPF
White blood cell (WBC) count 3–4/HPF
Protein 1+
Cast RBC casts
Glucose absent
Crystal none
Ketone absent
Nitrite absent
24 h urine protein excretion 0.6 g
HPF: high-power field
Which of the following would best describe the light microscopy findings in this case?

                    ### Options

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 12-year-old girl, including cola-colored urine, mild facial puffiness, and a recent sore throat, suggests a diagnosis of post-infectious glomerulonephritis, likely following a streptococcal infection. The urinalysis findings of hematuria (indicated by RBC casts) and mild proteinuria support this diagnosis. In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, light microscopy typically reveals hypercellular and enlarged glomeruli due to an increase in glomerular cells in response to inflammation. This aligns with the consensus that hypercellularity is a hallmark of this condition. Therefore, the best description of the light microscopy findings in this case is 'hypercellular and enlarged glomeruli.'
